<reason>B wins a competitive debate by controlling the endgame. A argued well: the category-error frame, "strict liability with extra steps," and the closing dilemma (the motion is either negligence-with-a-label or insurer-of-everything) were sharp and honestly defended, and A answered both of B's pressure forks directly ("yes, under negligence"). But B's framework — comparative fault for joint causation, risk-utility doctrine for multi-use products, and a defect defined as documented risk plus skipped feasible precaution — answered each of A's mechanisms with plausible law, and B dissolved the hospital/teenager bind coherently (duty tracks control; discharge by real warnings; shared blame). Crucially, B's Q2 fork forced A's concession that a provider ignoring documented flags should pay, and B's closing converted that into the debate's decisive framing: what remains is the legal vehicle, and B gave the better account of why the vehicle matters (enforceability without privity or a republisher, burden centered on the maker's own testing). A landed real hits — B overstated negligence's discovery limits, and B's Rebuttal 2 claim that its questions were "unanswered" was procedurally unfair since A's answering turn had not yet occurred — but B recovered in the closing and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Pressure Questions exchange decided the debate's shape: B's Q2 ("is there any documented-flag case where the provider pays? yes concedes the motion, no defends immunity") forced A's honest "yes, under negligence," which B's closing converted into "what remains is a quarrel over the label" — while A's counter ("recklessness was never the issue; treating every general model as a defective product is") was the sharpest single clash, leaving B's vehicle-matters argument as the surviving difference.</best_rebuttal>
